title: Physiology, Albumin -- Introduction
content: Albumin is the most abundant circulating protein in plasma. This molecule accounts for approximately half of the total plasma protein content (3.5-5 g/dL) in healthy humans. Hepatocytes in the liver synthesize albumin and rapidly release it into the bloodstream at a rate of 10 g to 15 g per day. Minimal albumin is stored in the liver, with the majority entering the circulation rapidly. In humans, serum albumin is a major modulator of plasma oncotic pressure and a transporter of endogenous and exogenous ligands, including drugs. Albumin is a water-soluble, nonimmunogenic protein characterized by a long half-life, low toxicity, and high stability.[ Hutapea et al , 2023]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Introduction
content: In clinical medicine, serum albumin is measured using standard serum laboratory testing. This parameter has been advocated as a marker of nutritional status. [1] Albumin serves as a colloid solution for fluid resuscitation, particularly in the setting of trauma (ie, hypovolemic shock) or large-volume paracentesis. [2] When interpreted as a laboratory measurement, serum albumin aids clinicians by providing insight into liver function and the capacity for protein biosynthesis and the production of factors essential to total-body homeostasis. [3] [4] [5]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Issues of Concern
content: A 2017 meta-analysis of low serum albumin levels in orthopedic populations found a 2.5-fold increase in the risk of surgical site infection across a range of interventions. Procedures evaluated included femur fracture management in trauma settings, including femoral neck fractures, total knee arthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty, and spinal operations involving fusion, decompression, metastatic disease, and spondylectomy. Serum albumin concentrations less than 3.5 g/dL were associated with the increased risk described.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Cellular Level -- Transcription
content: The human albumin gene ( ALB ) is a protein-coding locus on chromosome 4 that is highly expressed in hepatocytes and encodes the predominant plasma protein. Transcription initiates at multiple start sites within the 5′ flanking region, which contains conserved promoter elements such as TATA and CAAT boxes and facilitates efficient recruitment of RNA polymerase II. At least 2 transcription initiation sites and 2 polyadenylation signals are utilized differentially during pre-mRNA processing. The primary ALB transcript undergoes canonical splicing to remove introns and generate mature mRNA, which is translated into the preproalbumin precursor. Genomic organization, including flanking sequences, influences tissue-specific and constitutive expression of albumin in the liver. [6]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Cellular Level -- Synthesis
content: Human albumin is synthesized in hepatocytes as preproalbumin and modified to proalbumin within the endoplasmic reticulum. The N-terminal 6-amino acid peptide is cleaved by the furin enzyme in Golgi vesicles, producing mature serum albumin, a single-chain protein of 585 residues with an estimated molecular weight of 66,438 kDa. [7] Fully processed albumin is secreted constitutively from hepatocytes without significant intracellular storage, entering the bloodstream continuously. Nascent albumin becomes detectable in circulation within 30 to 60 minutes of Golgi processing. [8] During its 28- to 30-day lifespan, albumin may undergo various modifications that influence its functions.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Cellular Level -- Binding Sites
content: Human albumin is a small globular protein with 3 repeated homologous domains, each containing 2 distinct subdomains, A and B (see Image . Human Serum Albumin Structure). The monomeric protein has multiple drug-binding sites, with Sudlow sites I and II being the most prominent.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Cellular Level -- Binding Sites
content: Site I, located primarily in subdomain IIA with contributions from IIB and IIIA, binds bulky, negatively charged molecules such as warfarin. This site is flexible and can accommodate multiple ligands simultaneously, with 2 polar clusters formed by residues including Tyr150, His242, Arg257, Lys195, Lys199, Arg218, and Arg222. Site II, in subdomain IIIA, comprises a hydrophobic cleft with a polar patch near the entrance that accommodates smaller, aromatic carboxylic acids such as diazepam and ibuprofen. This site is narrower and more selective, and it exhibits stereoselectivity, unlike site I. A third binding site, site III (subdomain IB), binds bilirubin, hemin, fusidic acid, and sulfonamides; secondary sites are also present.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Cellular Level -- Binding Sites
content: Human serum albumin can bind up to 9 long-chain fatty acids, with asymmetric distribution across the protein. The first binding site, FA1, is located in subdomain IB and overlaps with the heme pocket. The second, FA2, lies between IA and IIA and stabilizes the protein's conformation. FA3 and FA4 coincide with Sudlow site II, while FA5 through FA9 occupy subdomains IIIB, IIA-IIB, and interdomain regions. Fatty acid binding influences drug transport, increasing plasma solubility and drug half-life while reducing free active drug concentrations. Albumin also binds thyroxine at 4 sites that overlap fatty acid–binding pockets, bacterial surface proteins through the protein A–related albumin-binding protein, and various metal ions—including magnesium, zinc, cadmium, and copper—at the N-terminal region, the free thiol of Cys34, and specific residues within the primary cadmium-binding site. Albumin also forms a complex with bilirubin near FA1.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Cellular Level -- Allosteric Modulation
content: Human serum albumin undergoes conformational changes upon ligand binding. Drugs, fatty acids, heme, and anesthetics can allosterically modulate binding at other sites. Fatty acid binding, particularly by long-chain molecules such as myristate, induces domain rearrangements that alter drug-site affinities. Ambient pH also affects protein structure, with acidic, neutral, and basic forms showing differing solubility, α-helical content, and ligand-binding properties.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Organ Systems Involved
content: Albumin is typically present in the intravascular compartment, interstitial space, and body fluids, such as cerebrospinal fluid. Elevated albumin concentrations in fluids such as ascites or urine often indicate underlying pathology.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Function
content: Human serum albumin is the primary modulator of plasma oncotic pressure and, as noted, serves as a transporter for various substances termed "ligands." Examples of endogenous ligands include bilirubin, ions, and fatty acids, while exogenous ligands include drugs. Pharmacologically active substances transported by albumin include, but are not limited to, methadone, propranolol, thiopental, furosemide, warfarin, methotrexate, and alfentanil. Severe liver disease can cause hypoalbuminemia, reducing the number of available binding sites for exogenous drugs. Reduced binding capacity leads to increased concentrations of unbound drugs, thereby increasing drug sensitivity. Drug sensitivity is particularly evident when serum albumin concentrations fall below 2.5 g/dL.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Function
content: Once albumin enters the circulation, approximately 30% to 40% remains in the bloodstream, with the remainder distributed into the interstitial space. Most proteins exiting the circulation are returned via the lymphatic system. The circulatory half-life of albumin is 16 hours. Most of albumin’s osmotic effect is attributed to its large molecular weight, while the remainder is thought to result from its negative charge. This negative charge enables albumin to attract cationic substances and water into the intravascular compartment. By modulating oncotic pressure, albumin significantly affects capillary membrane pressure, as shown in the following equation, where CP is capillary membrane pressure, HPc is capillary hydrostatic pressure, HPi is interstitial hydrostatic pressure, r is the reflection coefficient, OPc is capillary oncotic pressure, and OPi is interstitial oncotic pressure: CP = (HPc - HPi) - r(OPc - OPi)

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Function
content: Albumin accelerates wound healing and provides antioxidant effects. This molecule is a well-established circulatory protein with applications in advanced drug delivery. [9] Albumin nanoparticles have emerged as a promising drug-delivery platform, offering biocompatibility, controlled degradation, and targeting potential, particularly for inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer. [10] Human albumin significantly reduces the incidence of hyponatremia and postparacentesis circulatory dysfunction in individuals with liver cirrhosis. [11]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Pathophysiology
content: Hepatic albumin synthesis is a low-priority process, occurring when nutritional status is adequate. This process is inhibited by malnutrition, inflammation, hepatotoxin exposure, and elevated colloid osmotic pressure.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance
content: Human serum albumin is a standard laboratory biomarker in clinical medicine and is used as a colloid. Bovine serum albumin serves as a laboratory standard. [12] [13] [14]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin as a Laboratory Test
content: The liver’s biosynthetic capacity, reflected by serum albumin concentration, provides an indicator of hepatic function. Albumin measurement is often combined with prothrombin time or international normalized ratio to more comprehensively assess liver biosynthesis. Serum albumin values can remain normal in chronic liver disease and abnormal in cases of intact liver function. Evaluations of patients undergoing gastric bypass, liver pathology assessment, and liver function testing demonstrated poor correlation among these measures. Hypoalbuminemia may result from reduced albumin synthesis or dilution relative to free fluid. Dilutional hypoalbuminemia occurs in hepatic failure with ascites, as well as in renal or congestive heart failure. Clinical context must be considered during evaluation and diagnostic workup.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin as a Laboratory Test
content: Malnutrition can result in hypoalbuminemia. Fasting produces rapid effects, with albumin levels decreasing by approximately one-third within 24 to 48 hours. Albumin synthesis by the liver is restored quickly upon nutritional replenishment, typically within 15 to 30 minutes. Malnutrition is associated with adverse postsurgical outcomes and is commonly assessed to guide nutritional optimization and surgical readiness. Albumin is 1 of several laboratory measurements used to evaluate nutritional status. Other measurements include prealbumin, transferrin, and retinol-binding protein. None of these measurements is sufficient alone, and they must be interpreted alongside physical examination findings. Detection of hypoalbuminemia also helps in the diagnosis and monitoring of anasarca and malabsorption.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin as a Laboratory Test
content: Decreased albumin concentrations are associated with various conditions, including inflammatory disorders. This reduction may result from downregulation of albumin mRNA expression in the liver, leading to impaired synthesis, increased catabolism, and elevated vascular permeability. [15] Albumin aids in the evaluation of patients with peritoneal fluid accumulation (ascites). Causes of this manifestation include congestive heart failure, liver failure, and malignancy. Diagnostic paracentesis allows the collection of ascitic fluid, comparison of albumin concentration in the fluid with serum albumin, and calculation of the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG), represented by the following equation: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin as a Laboratory Test
content: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or greater indicates ascites due to a portal hypertensive etiology, such as congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, or alcoholic hepatitis. A SAAG less than 1.1 g/dL suggests ascites of nonportal hypertensive etiology, including peritoneal carcinomatosis, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis, or serositis.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin as a Colloid Fluid
content: The clinical use of albumin as a colloid fluid in critically ill individuals remains debated. Albumin persists longer in the intravascular compartment than crystalloids, theoretically reducing the risk of pulmonary edema. However, clinical trials have not demonstrated clear benefits of albumin over crystalloids, such as lactated Ringer solution or normal saline. The higher cost of albumin compared with crystalloids is also a consideration. In hypovolemic shock, the primary consideration is the type of fluid lost. For example, hemorrhagic shock from a gunshot wound requires packed red blood cells as a priority. Albumin may theoretically increase oncotic pressure, but its short half-life limits sustained effects.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin as a Colloid Fluid
content: The principal advantage of albumin over crystalloids is the increase in intravascular oncotic pressure. This effect may be beneficial in certain clinical scenarios. In individuals with cirrhosis undergoing large-volume paracentesis (ie, >5 L), administration of 6 to 8 g of albumin per liter of ascitic fluid drained may reduce the incidence of hemodynamic compromise. However, a recent systematic review found no mortality benefit from albumin administration after large-volume paracentesis in cirrhotic patients without hepatocellular carcinoma. Additional studies are required to confirm or refute these findings.

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Serum Albumin and Wound Complications in Orthopedic Surgery
content: Surgical site infection (SSI) is a common postoperative complication across orthopedic surgery, including spine surgery, elective total joint replacement, and trauma cases. Serum albumin concentrations below 3.5 g/dL are associated with an increased risk of SSI following these procedures. In elective total hip arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty, which demonstrate variable reproducibility and generally favorable short- and long-term outcomes in appropriately selected individuals, nutritional status is frequently considered prior to surgery. [16] [17] [18] [19] [20]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Congenital Analbuminemia
content: Errors in ALB transcription or pre-mRNA processing can generate aberrant transcripts that result in premature stop codons or exon skipping, yielding truncated or nonfunctional albumin. Such defective transcripts fail to produce normal circulating albumin, resulting in congenital analbuminemia, a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extremely low or absent serum albumin. Documented clinical manifestations include peripheral edema, hypotension, hyperlipidemia, fatigue, delayed wound healing, altered drug pharmacokinetics, and compensatory increases in other plasma proteins. These transcription or processing defects arise from splicing errors or frameshift mutations at critical splice sites, disrupting mRNA structure and protein translation. Molecular analysis of ALB variants highlights the impact of transcriptional errors on protein synthesis and phenotype. [21]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Clinical Pharmacokinetic Consequences of Altered Albumin Levels
content: Altered albumin function or concentration significantly affects drug pharmacokinetics, particularly for highly protein-bound medications. As noted, albumin is the major plasma carrier for many drugs, and lower albumin levels reduce the number of available binding sites, thereby increasing the proportion of unbound drug that is pharmacologically active and subject to tissue distribution and elimination. Hypoalbuminemia can increase apparent volume of distribution and alter clearance, potentially requiring therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment to avoid toxicity or subtherapeutic exposure. These effects are particularly relevant for highly albumin-bound agents, such as β-lactam antibiotics and antiepileptics, in which changes in protein binding influence efficacy and safety. [22]

title: Physiology, Albumin -- Clinical Significance -- Clinical Pharmacokinetic Consequences of Altered Albumin Levels
content: True hyperalbuminemia, ie, elevated serum albumin due to increased total albumin mass, is extremely rare. Most instances of high measured albumin reflect hemoconcentration due to dehydration or volume depletion, rather than increased synthesis. In clinical practice, albumin concentrations above the normal range typically result from reduced plasma water rather than a primary liver overproduction, and levels often normalize with rehydration. Persistent elevation after correction of volume status warrants evaluation for laboratory artifact or uncommon causes. Interpretation should consider the overall clinical context. [23]
